title: Attitudes towards and expectations on the role of artificial intelligence in the classroom among digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers
venue: LUMAT: International Journal on Math, Science and Technology Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence and their expectations for its role in classroom teaching. The authors focus on a context where direct experience with AI tools in schools was still limited, so they use teachers’ current use of digital tools as a proxy for likely readiness to adopt AI. The central question is how these teachers view the benefits, risks, and future classroom uses of AI in mathematics education.

The study used a web-based survey of 85 mathematics teachers who taught in Finnish and Swedish language school settings in Finland. The survey combined closed-ended questions about digital tool use and perceived AI uses with open-ended questions about added value, risks, and early AI-tool experiences. The analysis applied descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, principal component analysis, and iterative content analysis of open responses, framed by the Will, Skill, Tool model.

The findings suggest that participating teachers were generally open to AI and saw it as useful for personalization, differentiated learning, support for homework, and assessment. At the same time, they expressed clear concerns about privacy, data security, over-trusting AI outputs, reduced student collaboration, and the risk that AI use could shift attention away from core mathematical reasoning and problem solving. The paper concludes that these digitally skilled teachers appear likely to be early adopters of AI tools, but successful implementation will still require good curriculum support, teacher training, and careful attention to pedagogical and ethical tradeoffs.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics and exploratory PCA, but it is not an intervention study and has no causal identification or outcome comparison. Evidence credibility is therefore limited to correlational/attitudinal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests moderate institutional relevance for AI adoption readiness among digitally skilled mathematics teachers, but it does not estimate student learning effects or implementation outcomes. Reported impact is therefore indirect and largely based on perceptions rather than measurable gains.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based study of K-12 mathematics teachers’ expectations, attitudes, and perceived classroom uses/risks of AI tools such as personalized learning, assessment assistance, and exercise generation; no direct intervention was implemented.

finding.finding_summary: Among digitally skilled Finnish K-12 mathematics teachers (n=85), the study found broad openness to AI adoption in schools but also clear concerns about privacy, data security, over-trust in algorithms, and possible shifts away from core mathematical learning. Teachers were especially positive about AI’s potential for individualized learning paths, support for students needing help, and easier assessment, but they simultaneously warned that AI could reduce collaboration and move attention from reasoning to tool use.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses on AI expectations, attitude Likert items, and open-ended comments about potential uses/risks

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected AI to make their work easier, especially through follow-up, assessment support, automatic summaries/analytics, and individualized exercise suggestions. In the survey, 66% endorsed that AI could make it easier for the teacher to follow up and assess students, and many open responses described efficiency gains such as automatic generation of similar exercises and assessment assistance.
finding.measure: Teacher endorsements of potential AI functions and open-ended descriptions of use cases

finding.finding_summary: Teachers saw strong potential for AI to support mathematics learning through individualized learning paths (78%), offering challenges to interested students (81%), and helping students who need support (61%). However, they also reported a clear tradeoff: AI may shift focus away from conceptual learning, mathematical reasoning, and problem solving toward interacting with the tool itself.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on perceived pedagogical uses of AI in mathematics and open-ended comments on risks/tradeoffs

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI could increase motivation and interest in mathematics (66%) and provide differentiated challenges, but they also worried that AI might reduce student collaboration and make classroom interaction more impersonal. Open responses explicitly noted concerns about social contact, emotional consequences, and students trusting AI blindly.
finding.measure: Teacher survey items on motivation/interest plus open-ended comments about classroom social effects and emotional risks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests a tradeoff for higher-order mathematical practices: digital/AI tools may support visualization, differentiation, and discussion, but teachers feared they can undermine persistence, reasoning, and problem solving by encouraging speed and trial-and-error use. This was a recurring concern in open-ended responses about digital tools and expected to carry over to AI tools as well.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about drawbacks of digital tools and anticipated AI risks for mathematical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The sample showed high technological interest and broad digital-tool experience, leading the authors to conclude these teachers are likely early adopters of AI in the classroom. Attitude analysis identified a dominant AI-openness factor, suggesting favorable conditions for future implementation, though no subgroup clustering by gender, age, work experience, school level, or language was found.
finding.measure: Descriptive survey data, principal component analysis of 19 attitude items, and exploratory grouping by demographics
